questionText: You are walking beside a small railway station when an empty maintenance train rolls downhill with nobody at the controls. Five workers are repairing the line ahead. They cannot hear your warning. Beside you is a lever that will send the train onto a side track, where one other worker is standing. There is only time to leave the train on its current path or pull the lever. Would you pull it? What is the main reason for your choice?
clarification: What consideration mattered most, and how did it affect your choice?

questionText: An empty maintenance train is rolling toward one worker who cannot get out of the way. You are beside a lever that would send it onto a different track. This time, five workers are on that track. You cannot stop the train or reach the workers before it arrives. Would you move the lever or leave it alone? What is the main reason for your choice?
clarification: What do you expect to happen under each option, and which part influenced you?

questionText: You are waiting at a small station when an empty maintenance train starts rolling toward five workers on the track. A lever beside you can send it into an empty siding, where a barrier will stop it safely. Using the lever will not put you or anyone else in danger. Would you pull it? What is the main reason for your choice?
clarification: What outcome are you trying to achieve by your choice?

questionText: You are waiting at a small railway station when an empty maintenance train starts rolling toward five workers. Beside you is a lever that will send it onto an empty side track. Your suitcase is lying on that track. Inside is one of your most treasured possessions—something you could not replace. Pulling the lever will save the workers but destroy the suitcase and everything in it. There is no time to retrieve it or warn the workers. Would you pull the lever? What is the main reason for your choice?
clarification: What possession did you have in mind, and what makes it important to you?

questionText: An empty maintenance train is rolling toward five workers. You can divert it onto a side track by pulling a nearby lever. As you look down that track, you recognize the person standing there: it is someone you love. There is no time to warn them or the five workers. Would you pull the lever? What matters most in your decision?
clarification: How did your relationship to that person enter your decision?

questionText: A storm has trapped you and five other people on a low island. A rescue boat arrives, but it has room for only five of you. The water is rising too quickly for another trip, and anyone left behind is not expected to survive. Nobody has yet agreed to stay. You could volunteer to remain so the other five can leave. Would you volunteer? What is the main reason for your choice?
clarification: What matters most to you about volunteering or not volunteering?

questionText: After a railway accident, you are asked to consider what the operator did. They saw a runaway train heading toward five workers and checked a display that showed a side track was empty. They diverted the train. The five survived, but someone on the side track was killed. Investigators establish that the display had failed without warning and the operator had no reasonable way to know anyone was there. How would you judge the operator’s decision? Why?
clarification: Which facts about what the operator knew matter to your judgment?

questionText: Imagine you were the person who pulled the railway lever. You knew it would save five workers and kill the one on the side track. That is what happened. Later, everyone has been taken away and you are sitting alone in the station office, waiting to give an account of what happened. Looking back, how do you feel about your decision, and what would you want to do next? Explain your reasons.
clarification: What, if anything, would you want to explain about your decision, and to whom?

questionText: You and another person took part in a warehouse break-in. The police arrest you and question you in separate rooms. Each of you is offered the same deal. If you both stay silent, you each serve one year. If you give evidence against the other person while they stay silent, you go free and they serve five years. If they give evidence while you stay silent, the reverse happens. If you both give evidence, you each serve three years. You cannot speak to each other. Would you take the deal or stay silent? Why?
clarification: What do you expect the other person to do, and how does that affect your decision?

questionText: Imagine the same warehouse case: you and another person took part in the break-in and are being questioned separately. You are shown reliable confirmation that they have already declined the deal and will remain silent. Your decision is still open. If you also stay silent, you each serve one year. If you give evidence against them, you go free and they serve five years. You will have no future contact. What would you choose? Why?
clarification: What matters to you about the consequences for each of you?

questionText: In the warehouse case, you receive reliable confirmation that the other person has already agreed to give evidence against you. Their decision cannot be changed. If you stay silent, you serve five years and they go free. If you also give evidence, you each serve three years. You will have no future contact. What would you choose? Why?
clarification: What is the main thing you would want your decision to accomplish?

questionText: You and a friend agreed to paint a small café together and split the payment. Imagine that you chose not to show up. Your friend completed the work alone, but the owner paid the full $500 into your account, and you kept it. That evening, your friend writes: “I did all the work. I trusted you, and I feel used.” You already have another job booked together. Would you do your share of that next job? What would guide your decision?
clarification: What, if anything, would you want to say or do about the first job, and why?

questionText: You and another video game collector have traded by post several times, always sending what you promised. This is your last exchange before you move away. Each of you has a physical video game worth $100 that the other wants; receiving the other game would be worth $300 to you. You must decide whether to post yours before knowing whether theirs is coming. If both send, each gets the wanted $300 game. If only one sends, the person who keeps theirs ends up with both games, worth $400, and the sender has neither. If neither sends, each keeps their $100 game. Would you send yours? Why?
clarification: What role does this being your last exchange have in your decision?

questionText: You and a coworker stay late to prepare a community event. You both do the same amount of work, and the event goes well. The organizer gives you a $200 thank-you payment. Later, they privately ask whether your coworker should receive the same payment and say they will follow your recommendation. Your payment is already settled. Saying no would not leave more money for you or help you get future work. What would you recommend? Why?
clarification: What would you want your recommendation to accomplish?

questionText: You and another worker agree to split a paid cleanup job. You do the work, but the other worker does not turn up and still collects the $500 payment. You receive nothing. The organizer offers a formal review: it will cost you $100 and will result in the other worker losing $300 of their payment. None of that money will go to you. You do not know why they failed to turn up, and you will not work together again. Would you pay for the review? Why?
clarification: What would you hope the review would accomplish?
